A 6.35 mm TS plug fits a TRS jack. In a balanced input it ties the cold leg to ground, and the signal arrives unbalanced.

A Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS/3.5mm plug reaches a 6.35 mm jack through an adapter with a 3.5 mm TRS jack on one end and a 6.35 mm TRS plug on the other. The adapter keeps the stereo wiring: left on the tip, right on the ring.

A balanced mono input reads such an adapter as left minus right, so sound panned to the center cancels. A stereo source reaches balanced mono inputs through a 3.5 mm TRS to dual 6.35 mm TS cable, with each plug in its own input.
Two contacts, one insulating ring. The tip carries a single unbalanced signal; the sleeve is its ground return.

What is the difference between an Audio/Connector/Line/Out/Port and an Audio/Connector/Headphone/Port, and how do they differ on the Zoom H5?
What is the difference between an Audio/Connector/Line/Out/Port and an Audio/Connector/Headphone/Port, and how do they differ on the Zoom H5?

Short answer: a line out hands a signal to another device's input; a headphone out hands a signal to a pair of transducers. A headphone jack is a line out with a small power amplifier and a volume control in front of it. On the Zoom H5 the two are separate Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS/3.5mm jacks with independent level controls, so the recorder can feed a camera or an interface at a steady level while headphone volume moves freely.
What is the difference between an Audio/Connector/Line/Out/Port and an Audio/Connector/Headphone/Port, and how do they differ on the Zoom H5?
What is the difference between an Audio/Connector/Line/Out/Port and an Audio/Connector/Headphone/Port, and how do they differ on the Zoom H5?

The distinction is about current, not voltage. Both jacks swing about a volt. Only the headphone amplifier can push that voltage into a 32 Ω load without collapsing, which is why a line out asked to drive headphones goes quiet and loses its bottom end: the low impedance of the headphones loads the output stage down.

Headphone out into a line in works, and is the everyday field rig. The cost is that one knob now sets two things — turn the monitoring down and the recording gets quieter. A headphone amplifier is also noisier and clips earlier than the line stage on the same device.

What is the difference between an Audio/Connector/Line/Out/Port and an Audio/Connector/Headphone/Port, and how do they differ on the Zoom H5?

Answer/Official from the H5 Operation Manual: LINE OUT LEVEL sits under the IN/OUT menu and runs from −30 to 0 dB. Its stated purpose is feeding "the external mic input jack on an SLR camera or other jack with a high input gain" without an attenuator cable in the line — the H5 pads its own line out rather than asking for a resistive cable.

The manual is explicit that the two outputs are independent: the LINE OUT LEVEL setting "does not affect the level output from the PHONE jack." That independence is the practical payoff, and it is what makes a simultaneous send-and-monitor rig possible on this recorder.

Both jacks are live at once, so a single H5 can feed a camera or interface from LINE OUT while the performer or engineer monitors on PHONE.

A coaxial connector carrying one signal: a center pin for the signal, an outer shell for ground and shield. Every channel needs its own connector, so a stereo pair takes two and component video takes three.
Also called a phono connector, after its first job of wiring a phonograph into a radio receiver, and cinch in France and Germany after the Chicago manufacturer of that name.

Introduced by the Radio Corporation of America by 1937 inside the model U-109 radio-phonograph, and on the rear panels of its radios by 1938. Through the 1950s it displaced the 6.35 mm phone connector across consumer hi-fi.
Never formally specified. Compatibility rests on manufacturers matching each other, which is why plug impedance varies and composite video over RCA matches 75 Ω only loosely.
Audio/Connector/RCA/Stereo — a pair carrying unbalanced analog stereo.
RCA/Connector/Ref/Index — color coding across audio and video, and the plug and jack pages.
Two Audio/Connector/RCA connectors wired as one unbalanced analog stereo line, one per channel.
Line level throughout — the usual link from a turntable preamp, CD player or mixer into an amplifier or a powered monitor.
Plug center pin: 1/8 in (3.175 mm) diameter
Plug outer shell: 1/3 in (8.47 mm) diameter
Red is the right channel in every convention. The left channel is white, black or grey depending on the maker.
Turntable, CD player and tape deck outputs into an amplifier or receiver
Line input on powered studio monitors, such as IK Multimedia/iLoud Micro Monitors
Mixer main outs into a recorder
Breakout cables carry an Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS/3.5mm plug on one end and the RCA pair on the other, tip to left and ring to right.
The signal pin meets the jack before the shells ground, so connecting a live pair hums or buzzes when the two devices share no ground. The same happens when a plug works its way half out.
A round, latching connector with three pins that carries one Audio/Balanced audio signal. It is the standard connector for microphones and for line connections between pro gear.
The 3-pin version is the audio one. 4-, 5- and more-pin versions exist for intercom, DMX lighting and stereo, and don't mate with it.
About 19 mm across, with a metal shell around the pins.
A latch on the female connector locks the male in place. Pressing the release tab frees it.
Pin 1 is longer than pins 2 and 3, so ground connects first when a plug goes in.
Pin 2 — hot, the signal in its normal polarity.
Pin 3 — cold, the signal in reverse polarity.
Audio/Phantom Power rides on pins 2 and 3 together, with pin 1 as its return.
Mic inputs on mixers, recorders and audio interfaces. Signal flows from the male connector on the mic into the female socket on the input.
Balanced line outputs on larger mixers and powered speakers.
The output of a Audio/DI Box.
A combo jack takes either an XLR plug or a 1/4" Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS/6.35mm plug in one socket, as on Zoom H5/UI/Area/4-Bottom/1-Input-1-Jack.
XLR-to-TRS cables keep the balanced wiring: tip to pin 2, ring to pin 3, sleeve to pin 1.
A voltage level in decibels relative to 0.775 V RMS, the voltage that delivers 1 mW into 600 Ω.
+4 dBu (about 1.23 V) is pro line level. Consumer line level is −10 dBV, about −7.8 dBu, where dBV is relative to 1 V.
